{
 "cells": [
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "We follow up on [first](./01_spin_half_Rabi_Hahn.ipynb) tutorial, but with a more concrete quantum system: the nitrogen vacancy (NV) center in diamond. NVs are the most known color centers, due to its extensive research in quantum technologies. Here, however, we will focus on QuaCCAToo's usage rather than the physics of the NV itself. For more detailed information about NVs, we recommend:\n",
    "\n",
    "[1] E. V. Levine, et al., Principles and techniques of the quantum diamond microscope, Nanophotonics 8, 1945 (2019).\n",
    "\n",
    "[2] S. Pezzagna and J. Meijer, Quantum computer based on color centers in diamond, Applied Physics Reviews 8,011308 (2021)."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 1,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "import numpy as np\n",
    "from lmfit import Model\n",
    "import copy\n",
    "from qutip import fock_dm, tensor, qeye, jmat\n",
    "\n",
    "from quaccatoo import plot_energy_B0, NV, Rabi, Ramsey, PMR, RabiModel, fit_two_lorentz_sym, fit_two_sinc2_sym, Analysis, ExpData"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "# 1. Energy Levels"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "We begin defining the quantum system from the predefined `NV` class in quaccatoo. The class has only two mandatory parameters, the nitrogen isotope $^{14}\\text{N}$, $^{15}\\text{N}$ or None (which neglects all nuclear terms) and the magnetic field in mT. Optionally, the user can define a misalignment angle between the NV axis and the magnetic field, alternative magnetic field units, alternative Hamiltonian units, or collapse operators for the pulsed experiments. To visualize the energy levels, we use the `plot_energy` method."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 2,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 200x600 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "qsys_1 = NV(\n",
    "    N = 15,\n",
    "    B0 = 38.4,\n",
    "    units_B0 = 'mT'    \n",
    ")\n",
    "\n",
    "qsys_1.plot_energy()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "We observe the three electronic energy levels of the NV center: $m_s=0,-1,+1$. To be able to see the nuclear levels splitting, we need to specify a smaller energy range in the `plot_energy` method."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 3,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 200x600 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "qsys_1.plot_energy(energy_lim=[1790, 1798])"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Now, the splitting from the $^{15}\\text{N}$ nuclear spin is observed.\n",
    "\n",
    "So far we considered $B_0=38.4$ mT, but if we want to see how these energy levels change as a function of the external magnetic field, we can use the `plot_energy_B0` function."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 4,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "# range of B0 values where we want to plot the energy levels\n",
    "B0_array = np.linspace(0, 200, 100)\n",
    "\n",
    "plot_energy_B0(\n",
    "    B0 = B0_array,\n",
    "    # here we calculate the Hamiltonian for each B0 value\n",
    "    H0 = [NV(N=15, B0=B, units_B0='mT').H0 for B in B0_array] \n",
    ")"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "As expected, the $m_s=+1$ grows linearly with the field, while the $m_s=-1$ decreases linearly and $m_s=0$ level is not affected by the field. After 100 mT, the level anticrossing occurs.\n",
    "\n",
    "The energy levels also depend on the temperature, due to slight changes in the Zero-Field term. If the user want to specify a specific temperature, this can be done through the `temp` parameter with temperature units given by `units_temp`, which is by default set to Kelvin."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 5,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "name": "stderr",
     "output_type": "stream",
     "text": [
      "/tmp/ipykernel_31494/4129145445.py:1: UserWarning: The operational temperature range for the Hamiltonian model is between 5.6 K to 700 K. Results might be inaccurate.\n",
      "  NV(\n"
     ]
    },
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 200x600 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "NV(\n",
    "    N = 15,\n",
    "    B0 = 38.4,\n",
    "    units_B0 = 'mT',\n",
    "    temp = 3,\n",
    "    units_temp = 'K' \n",
    ").plot_energy()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Notice that the differece at $T=3$ K is really small as compared to room temperature. The operational temperature range for this Hamiltonian is between 2.5 K to 700 K."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "# 2. Rabi Oscillations of Electronic Spin"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Just like in the previous notebook, the first experiment usually conducted is Rabi oscillations. In this case, $\\hat{h}_1$ and the resonant frequency of the pulse are not as trivial as before. The user can define their own parameters, but the NV class has a standard interaction Hamiltonian\n",
    "$$ \\hat{h}_1 = \\hat{S}_x \\otimes \\mathbb{1}, $$\n",
    "which can be obtained by the `MW_h1` method. While the resonant frequencies for the $m_s=0 \\rightarrow -1$ and $m_s=0 \\rightarrow +1$ can be obtained from `MW_freqs` attribute, which takes the average between the two nuclear spin states. Again, we will consider a square cosine wave for the pulse."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 6,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "# typical NV Rabi frequency in MHz\n",
    "w1 = 16.72 \n",
    "\n",
    "rabi_sim_1 = Rabi(\n",
    "    # pulse duration in us\n",
    "    pulse_duration = np.arange(0, 0.15, 3e-3), \n",
    "    # NV center system defined above\n",
    "    system = qsys_1, \n",
    "    # control Hamiltonian\n",
    "    h1 = w1*qsys_1.MW_h1, \n",
    "    # MW frequency for the ms=0 --> ms=-1 state transition\n",
    "    pulse_params = {'f_pulse': qsys_1.MW_freqs[0]} \n",
    ")\n",
    "\n",
    "\n",
    "# run the experiment and plot results\n",
    "rabi_sim_1.run()\n",
    "rabi_analysis_1 = Analysis(rabi_sim_1)\n",
    "rabi_analysis_1.plot_results()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "If we want to compare with the simulation with experimental data, we can use the `ExpData` class to load it from .dat or .txt file and the `compare_with` method. In this case, the experimental data was measured for the same NV parameters as defined previously."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 7,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "LinregressResult(slope=np.float64(2.589543312483201), intercept=np.float64(-2.0453606037741343), rvalue=np.float64(0.9872724331132606), pvalue=np.float64(5.450830010921875e-40), stderr=np.float64(0.060209767213129525), intercept_stderr=np.float64(0.05996996938645169))"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 7,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    },
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "exp_data = ExpData(file_path='./exp_data_tutorials/Ex02_NV_rabi.dat',\n",
    "                    variable_column=0,\n",
    "                    results_columns=1,\n",
    "                    yerr_columns=2\n",
    "                   )\n",
    "# convert the variable from s to us\n",
    "exp_data.variable *= 1e6 \n",
    "\n",
    "rabi_analysis_1.compare_with(exp_data)\n",
    "rabi_analysis_1.plot_comparison()\n",
    "rabi_analysis_1.pearson"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "We observe a strong correlation of the simulation and experimental data with an rvalue of 0.987. The standard observable for the NV is the population in the $m_s=0$ given by the fluorescence. To see the populations of the other two states $m_s=\\pm 1$, we need to redefine the system observables and run again the Rabi experiment."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 8,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "qsys_1.observable = [tensor(fock_dm(3, 0), qeye(2)), tensor(fock_dm(3, 2), qeye(2))]\n",
    "\n",
    "# run the experiment\n",
    "rabi_sim_1.run()\n",
    "Analysis(rabi_sim_1).plot_results()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Note that population of the $m_s=+1$ remains 0, as we are using the $m_s=0 \\rightarrow -1$ resonant frequency, while the $m_s=-1$ population oscillates with the same frequency as the $m_s=0$ population, but with opposite sign. If we used the other resonant frequency, the $m_s=+1$ population would oscillate but $m_s=-1$ would remain 0."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 9,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "rabi_sim_2 = Rabi(\n",
    "    pulse_duration = np.linspace(0, 3/w1, 1000),\n",
    "    system = qsys_1,\n",
    "    h1 = w1*qsys_1.MW_h1,\n",
    "    # MW frequency for the ms=0 --> ms=+1 state transition\n",
    "    pulse_params = {'f_pulse': qsys_1.MW_freqs[1]} \n",
    ")\n",
    "\n",
    "rabi_sim_2.run()\n",
    "rabi_analysis_2 = Analysis(rabi_sim_2)\n",
    "rabi_analysis_2.plot_results()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Finally, by running a fit of the observable we can extract the $\\pi$-pulse duration."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 10,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/html": [

       "<lmfit.model.ModelResult at 0x7fe85a696900>"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 10,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    },
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",

      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "rabi_analysis_2.run_fit(\n",
    "    fit_model = RabiModel(),\n",
    "    # since there are two observables, we need to specify which one we want to fit\n",
    "    results_index = 0\n",
    "    )\n",
    "\n",
    "rabi_analysis_2.plot_fit()\n",
    "rabi_analysis_2.fit_params[0]"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "As expected the $\\pi$-pulse duration is very close to $1/(2\\omega_1)$."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "# 3. Ramsey Experiment"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## 3.1 Lab Frame"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "A simple, but important, pulse sequence in quantum sensing is the Ramsey experiment. It measures the accumulated phase difference in the two levels, by applying a $\\pi/2$ pulse, waiting for a time $\\tau$ and applying another $\\pi/2$ pulse, then measuring the population in the $m_s=0$ state."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 11,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "# NV center system same as before with standard observables\n",
    "qsys_2 = NV(\n",
    "    N=15,\n",
    "    B0 = 40,\n",
    "    units_B0='mT'\n",
    ")\n",
    "\n",
    "# Rabi frequency in MHz\n",
    "w1 = 30 \n",
    "\n",
    "ramsey_sim = Ramsey(\n",
    "    # free evolution time in us\n",
    "    free_duration = np.linspace(1/2/w1, 3, 500), \n",
    "    system = qsys_2,\n",
    "    pi_pulse_duration = 1/2/w1,\n",
    "    h1 = w1*qsys_2.MW_h1,\n",
    "    pulse_params = {'f_pulse': qsys_2.MW_freqs[0]}\n",
    ")\n",
    "\n",
    "ramsey_sim.plot_pulses(tau=.03)"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 12,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "ramsey_sim.run()\n",
    "Analysis(ramsey_sim).plot_results()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "We could fit the results again with a period oscillation, but to illustrate a different method we will use the FFT from quaccatoo. First, the FFT is run with `run_FFT` method, then the peaks are found with `get_peaks_FFT`."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 13,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "ramsey_analysis = Analysis(ramsey_sim)\n",
    "\n",
    "ramsey_analysis.run_FFT()\n",
    "ramsey_analysis.get_peaks_FFT()\n",
    "ramsey_analysis.plot_FFT(freq_lim=[0,5])"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "The frequencies are too spaced in the FFT due to the short range of $\\tau$, but we can see the main peak corresponds to approximately half of the hyperfine splitting of the nuclear spin $a_{||}/2=1.515$ MHz, as expected."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## 3.2 Rotating Frame"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Let's now try to simulate the same sequence with delta pulses through the rotation operator of\n",
    "$$\\hat{R}_x = \\begin{pmatrix}\n",
    "1 & 0 \\\\\n",
    "0 & \\hat{\\sigma}_x \\\\\n",
    "\\end{pmatrix} = \n",
    "\\begin{pmatrix}\n",
    "1 & 0 & 0\\\\\n",
    "0 & 0 & 1\\\\\n",
    "0 & 1 & 0\n",
    "\\end{pmatrix},\n",
    "$$\n",
    "which can be obtained through the `MW_Rx` attribute of the `NV` class. As in the previous tutorial, the simulation with delta pulses can be defined by setting `pi_pulse_duration = 0`."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 14,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "ramsey_delta_sim = Ramsey(\n",
    "    free_duration = np.linspace(0, 3, 1000), \n",
    "    system = qsys_2,\n",
    "    pi_pulse_duration = 0,\n",
    "    Rx = qsys_2.MW_Rx[0],\n",
    ")\n",
    "\n",
    "ramsey_delta_sim.plot_pulses(tau=.03)"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "In this case then, the delta pulses appear as vertical lines."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 15,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "ramsey_delta_sim.run()\n",
    "Analysis(ramsey_delta_sim).plot_results()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "The expectation value of the observable presents fast modulations, contrary to the previous case. This is because that by adopting delta pulses we are also assuming the rotating frame. Thus, the Hamiltonian $\\hat{H}_0$ needs to be modified accordingly. For that, we make a new quantum system, without the electronic terms and the perpendicular terms of the Hyperfine interaction."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 16,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "qsys_3 = copy.copy(qsys_2)\n",
    "qsys_3.H0 = (\n",
    "            3.03 * tensor(jmat(1, \"z\"), jmat(1 / 2, \"z\"))\n",
    "            + qsys_3.nuclear_zeeman()\n",
    "        )\n",
    "\n",
    "ramsey_delta_sim_2 = Ramsey(\n",
    "    free_duration = np.linspace(0, 3, 1000), \n",
    "    system = qsys_3,\n",
    "    pi_pulse_duration = 0,\n",
    "    Rx = qsys_3.MW_Rx[0],\n",
    ")\n",
    "\n",
    "ramsey_delta_sim_2.run()\n",
    "Analysis(ramsey_delta_sim_2).plot_results()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Where we not obtain the results from the laboratory frame."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "# 4. Pulsed Optically Detected Magnetic Resonance (pODMR)"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "To further study the energy levels of the system, we simulate a pODMR experiment. A pODMR experiment is simply composed by a pulse of varying frequency, thus when it corresponds to a resonance, a change in the observable is expected."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 17,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "podmr_sim_1 = PMR(\n",
    "    # frequencies to scan in MHz\n",
    "    frequencies = np.arange(1400, 4300, 10), \n",
    "    system = qsys_2,\n",
    "    pulse_duration = 1/2/w1,\n",
    "    h1 = w1*qsys_2.MW_h1\n",
    ")\n",
    "\n",
    "podmr_sim_1.run()\n",
    "Analysis(podmr_sim_1).plot_results()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Two resonances can be observed, corresponding to the two electronic spin transitions and with a splitting given by the Zeeman interaction with the external magnetic field. To see the nuclear spin splitting, we need to reduce the Rabi frequency to have a better spectral resolution."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 18,
   "metadata": {},
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "image/png": "",
      "text/plain": [
       "<Figure size 600x400 with 1 Axes>"
      ]
     },
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "display_data"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "w1 = 0.3\n",
    "\n",
    "podmr_sim_2 = PMR(\n",
    "    frequencies = np.arange(1745, 1753, 0.05),\n",
    "    system = qsys_2,\n",
    "    pulse_duration = 1/2/w1,\n",
    "    h1 = w1*qsys_2.MW_h1,\n",
    ")\n",
    "\n",
    "podmr_sim_2.run()\n",
    "Analysis(podmr_sim_2).plot_results()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "The two resonances now correspond to the two nuclear spin transitions. To get the splitting, we can fit them with Lorentzian Functions."
